title: Affiliate Programs: Check Geographic Eligibility and Visitor Routing Before Promotion
description: A webmaster checklist for comparing affiliate program country eligibility, destination behavior and reporting. Verify where referrals may be sent before building campaigns.
excerpt: A program may be a poor fit if its rules or destination behavior do not match your audience’s locations. Check eligible markets, redirects and fallback paths before promoting an offer.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish the locations where promotion is allowed from the locations where a visitor can complete the intended journey.
Check whether a referral link changes destination by location and how that behavior is documented.
Plan a clear fallback when the promoted destination is unavailable or unsuitable for a visitor.
Keep campaign notes that record the audience, approved traffic source and destination behavior you verified.

sections.heading: Map audience locations to program rules
paragraphs: A webmaster’s audience may be distributed across several countries or regions, while an affiliate program may define its own eligible markets and traffic rules. Do not assume that a destination accepting a visitor means the promotion is allowed, or that an approved promotion guarantees the destination is available everywhere. Compare the program’s written restrictions with the locations and traffic sources you actually serve. If the rules use terms that are unclear, request clarification before sending traffic from an uncertain market.

Build a basic market map for each campaign: where visitors are expected to come from, where the program permits promotion and where the destination appears intended to serve users. Avoid using general assumptions about regional access as evidence. Keep the map tied to the program’s current written terms and the destination information available to you. If your audience changes, revisit the fit rather than treating the original review as permanent.
bullets: List the visitor locations relevant to the campaign.
Record any stated country or region restrictions on promotion.
Separate promotion eligibility from destination availability.
Escalate unclear market rules before launching traffic.

sections.heading: Inspect link behavior from different locations
paragraphs: An affiliate link may lead to a general destination, a localized page or a route that depends on the visitor’s location. Verify the behavior using appropriate, permitted test methods and do not misrepresent a test location as ordinary user behavior. Note whether the destination, language, currency display or sign-up path changes. If the program’s documentation explains these variations, compare observed behavior with that explanation and report meaningful discrepancies through the program’s support route.

A redirect that works from one location does not establish that every visitor will see the same page. Test only within the program’s rules and your site’s privacy commitments. Keep a dated record of the link tested, the route observed and the context of the test. Avoid building a campaign around a redirect you cannot explain or monitor. Where a link can route visitors to an unexpected or irrelevant destination, treat that as an audience-fit issue rather than a minor technical detail.

table.caption: A geographic fit review separates four questions that are often conflated.
rows: May I promote to this market?
Exclude or proceed only within stated rules
Can visitors reach a relevant destination?
Documented destination availability and permitted checks
Choose an appropriate link or do not target the market
Explain or monitor the route before scaling
What if the destination is unavailable?
Program guidance and your own fallback page
Provide a clear alternative without misleading visitors

sections.heading: Plan language and destination expectations
paragraphs: A visitor may land on a page whose language or regional details differ from the page they expected. Check whether the program describes localized destinations and whether the link makes the intended transition understandable. Do not claim that a product, service or sign-up option is available in a particular market unless you have reliable, current evidence. Keep editorial copy modest and specific: describe what a visitor can expect from the link, and avoid promising access that the destination or program does not confirm.

If your own site serves readers in multiple languages, consider how the affiliate link fits into that experience. A translated article does not establish that the destination supports the same language. Where the destination may not match the reader’s language, make the transition clear or provide a non-commercial explanation of the limitation. The decision is about trust and fit, not maximizing the number of clicks sent to a destination.

sections.heading: Create a relevant fallback for unavailable destinations
paragraphs: A visitor should not be left with a confusing error or a misleading redirect when an offer is not suitable for their location. Ask whether the program provides a documented alternative destination or advises publishers how to handle unavailable markets. If it does not, consider whether your own page can explain that the link may not work for every visitor and point to neutral, relevant information. Do not attempt to bypass regional restrictions or send visitors to a substitute offer that does not match their intent.

Fallbacks should be reviewed as carefully as the primary link. Confirm that any alternative is permitted, relevant and clearly labeled. If there is no suitable permitted fallback, it may be better not to target that market with the offer. Record the reasoning so future editors do not reintroduce an unsuitable link during a content refresh. This is especially useful for evergreen pages whose audience or program terms can change over time.

sections.heading: Keep a market and link review record
paragraphs: A concise record makes future checks repeatable. Store the program terms or support clarification used, the markets considered, the link and destination behavior reviewed, and the date of the check. Note any limitations, unresolved questions and fallback decisions. Avoid storing unnecessary personal information about visitors; the review concerns campaign setup and program rules, not individual tracking beyond what is permitted and disclosed.

Revisit the review when the program changes its terms, the destination changes its market presentation, your audience geography shifts or a link begins routing differently. A sudden decline in referrals alone does not prove a geographic issue, so use evidence before changing campaign decisions. This record helps distinguish a permitted, documented setup from a guess and supports a more responsible comparison between programs.
bullets: Maintain a dated record of markets, restrictions and tested link behavior.
Document who clarified an ambiguous rule and what was confirmed.
Review links when terms or destination behavior change.
Do not route around restrictions or imply universal availability.

faqs.question: If a destination opens in a country, does that mean I may promote it there?
faqs.answer: No. Destination access and permission to promote are separate questions. Review the program’s written terms for the relevant market and ask for clarification when the rules do not clearly cover your traffic.

faqs.question: How often should a webmaster recheck geographic link behavior?
faqs.answer: Recheck when program terms, destination routing or audience markets change, and when you encounter a credible indication that a link behaves differently. Keep the date and method of each check so observations are not mistaken for permanent guarantees.

faqs.question: What should I do if a referral destination is not relevant to a visitor?
faqs.answer: Do not disguise the mismatch or bypass a restriction. Use a documented, permitted alternative if one exists, explain the limitation clearly, or avoid targeting that market with the offer.
